top_choice_rationale: The optical lattice clock combines an original idea (a magic wavelength that cancels the lattice light shift for many neutral atoms held in the Lamb-Dicke regime), a decisive experiment, and reproduction near the 10^-18 level by several independent laboratories and species. It has already yielded new physics such as millimetre-scale redshift tests, limits on drifting constants and dark matter, and many-body effects inside the clock. It is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes. The two-laureate allocation (Katori for concept and first realisation, Ye for record accuracy and many-body control) and the narrow citation are defensible, although the chronology rests on recollection and I cannot settle the Katori/Ye weighting from memory. A mature, well-scoped award is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; I have long-standing collaborations in attosecond physics (L'Huillier, Keller groups) and the atomic-theory community, but no documented tie to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups
